analysis.one_liner: Requires social media apps to build safer defaults for kids and lets users turn off personalized algorithms.
analysis.headline: 76 of 100 senators have signed on and the Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill on August 5, 2026, but it has not yet come up for a vote on the Senate floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill puts a legal duty on social media, gaming, messaging, and streaming platforms to design their products so they don't foreseeably harm minors under 17 — covering things like compulsive use, harassment, eating disorders, and sexual exploitation. It requires the highest privacy and safety settings to be on by default for kids, gives parents tools to see and control their child's account, bans advertising drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to minors, and stops platforms from running market research on children under 13. Separately, it requires any platform using a personalized algorithm to tell users and let them switch to a chronological, non-personalized feed. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 17 and their parents. Kids get the most protective privacy and safety settings turned on by default, an easy way to opt out of algorithmic feeds, restrictions on who can contact them and what data is public, and a platform obligation to respond to reports of harm within days. Parents get tools to view and manage their child's settings and time on the app. All users — adults included — gain the right to see content without an engagement-maximizing algorithm and get an independent annual audit of how big platforms treat minors.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must turn on the most protective privacy and safety settings by default for any user they know is a minor, including limits on who can contact them, restrictions on public visibility of their personal data, and notice when their location is tracked.

Minors get a prominently displayed option to opt out of personalized recommendation systems and switch to a chronological feed, and can turn off design features built to extend time on the app, like infinite scrolling and autoplay.

Platforms cannot advertise narcotic drugs, cannabis, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to any user they know is a minor, and must run market research on children under 13 at all — or on minors at all without parental consent.

Parents get tools to view and manage their child's privacy and account settings, restrict purchases, and see and cap total time spent on the platform, and these tools are on by default for known children under 13.

Platforms with over 10 million U.S. users must publish an annual public report based on an independent third-party audit covering how minors use the platform, how their data feeds recommendation systems, and whether the safeguards actually work.

Any platform using a personalized ranking algorithm must notify users and let them switch to a version that does not use their data — a protection that applies to adult users too — and cannot charge them more for choosing it.
The FTC and state attorneys general can sue platforms to enforce the safeguards, with penalties under the Federal Trade Commission Act.

analysis.who_pays: The large social media, gaming, messaging, and streaming companies that profit from engagement. They would carry compliance costs for safeguards, parental tools, annual third-party audits, and public transparency reports, and they would lose some of the design techniques and targeted advertising that keep minors on the app — minors' time and attention being the raw material of ad revenue. Smaller platforms face lighter duties: the audit requirement only applies above 10 million U.S. users, and report responses get more time under that threshold.

drawbacks.text: Because platforms face legal liability for foreseeable harms under the duty of care, they have an incentive to over-restrict: a platform may broadly limit what minors can see — including legitimate information about mental health, sexuality, or identity — rather than risk being sued. The bill bars enforcement based on the viewpoint of a user's protected speech, but it does not stop a platform from quietly restricting entire topics for minors.

The bill explicitly does not require platforms to verify users' ages, and says they need not collect any age data they don't already have. A platform can escape most obligations by claiming it does not know a user is a minor; the bill directs the Commerce Department to study device-level age verification for a year rather than mandate it.

The parental tools give parents visibility into and control over a child's account, which can be used to surveil a young person in an abusive or unsupportive home. The bill itself recognizes this risk and directs the FTC to issue guidance on safeguarding minors against the misuse of parental tools.

Ordinary families cannot sue on their own. Enforcement is left to the FTC and state attorneys general, and the bill bars using the core duty-of-care provision as the basis for a state-law lawsuit, so the strength of protection depends heavily on who holds those offices and how aggressively they act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to children and parents are concrete and the design — safe defaults, real parental tools, independent audits, an algorithm opt-out for everyone — is more specific than most internet bills. The main honest concerns are that the duty of care could make platforms over-censor what minors can see, and that without any age-verification requirement the rules only bite when a platform admits it knows a user is a minor. Those are real weaknesses, but they weaken the bill's enforcement rather than reversing who it serves.

outcome.mechanism: It's still waiting on the Senate floor: the Commerce Committee voted on August 5, 2026 to send the bill to the full Senate with changes, but leadership has not scheduled a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on May 14, 2025, joined by Senators Blumenthal, Thune, and Schumer, and it was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
It drew 76 cosponsors — 33 of 45 Senate Democrats, 42 of 55 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 independents — an unusually wide bipartisan base for an internet regulation bill.
On August 5, 2026, the Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, clearing it for possible Senate floor action.
As of the end of the record, the bill has not received a vote in the full Senate or the House, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the major social media platforms. With no law enacted, they continue to design for maximum engagement and to collect and monetize minors' data under the pre-existing rules, while the bipartisan coalition that supports the bill waits for floor time.

sides.party_line_note: Support spans both parties almost evenly: 33 of 45 Democrats, 42 of 55 Republicans, and 1 of 2 independents cosponsored, and the bill was introduced jointly by leaders of both parties.

industries.note: Platforms monetize minors' time and attention through engagement-maximizing design and targeted advertising, which the bill directly restricts through safe defaults, audits, and a duty of care around compulsive use. Every month without a law is revenue preserved under the old rules.

Online games are covered platforms: the bill restricts microtransactions to known minors, limits gameplay interruptions for safeguards, and bans advertising drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to minors. In-game purchases, including surprise-mechanics items, are squarely in scope.

The bill bans advertising certain regulated products to known minors and requires clear labeling of ads and paid endorsements shown to them, shrinking the targeted-advertising audience that minors represent.

Streaming services are covered, but the bill gives services whose programming is preselected by the provider a broad compliance shortcut — basic parental controls and an ad restriction rather than the full duty of care — so the burden on them is much lighter than on social platforms.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is in a strong procedural position in the Senate: a favorable committee report from August 2026 and cosponsorship from roughly three-quarters of the chamber make a floor vote realistic before the Congress ends in January 2027. The bigger hurdle is the House, which took no action on the near-identical version that passed the Senate 91-3 in the last Congress; without House passage the bill dies at adjournment no matter how the Senate votes.
